passage: The week before Diwali, the Pune school hall was hung with paper lanterns for the maths olympiad. Avni had solved every practice sheet at home, even the star questions. While they waited, Rafiq from the next row leaned over. 'My cousin says girls always get less in olympiads. It's science.' He said it lightly and turned back. Avni's stomach tightened into a knot. When the paper came, the first question was one she had done twice at home. She read it four times. What if he's right? What if everyone sees? Her pencil felt heavy. She skipped it, came back, rushed, made a silly mistake. At the bell she had left three questions blank, questions she knew. Walking out past the lanterns, her face burned.

qa.a: That girls always get less in olympiads.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling as she read the first question four times?
qa.a: Avni felt anxious and afraid of proving Rafiq's words true, a knot in her stomach that crowded out the problem.

qa.q: What could a teacher or parent say to Avni after the olympiad?
qa.a: They could remind her she solved the star questions at home, and explain that fear of a label, not lack of ability, made her freeze.

qa.a: Avni would likely have started calmly and solved the question she had done twice, without fear eating up her thinking.

Tarun joined on the sports quota, and some staff and students treat that as meaning he isn't academic. In our weekly practice sessions he is quick and accurate; last week he explained the electricity problems to Uma better than I could. But his mid-term score was 41. I watched him during the exam: he rushed the first page, kept erasing correct answers and looked up whenever anyone walked past his desk. Afterwards he said quietly, 'Everyone expects the cricket boy to fail.' His result does not reflect his ability. Next steps: a weekly low-stakes timed practice with him, framed as practice, not judgement; and I have asked the class teacher to stop the 'quota' jokes in class.

Robotics qualifier today. Fourteen teams, and I was the only girl coding. When the judge saw me at the laptop, he said, 'Oh! Is your brother helping?' He meant it as a joke. Anirban, my actual teammate (not my brother), laughed awkwardly. After that my brain went fuzzy. Anirban texted: 'You're the best coder on our team. That judge rattled you.' He's right.

passage: In the government school at Sikandarpur, Imran's science project on rainwater harvesting won first place at the block fair. Imran shrugged, but that evening he pushed his notebook under the bed. He stopped raising his hand. When his older sister Noor asked why he wasn't preparing for the district round, he mumbled, 'What's the point? They think I cheated anyway. If I don't try, nobody can say I failed.' Noor pulled the notebook out, dusted it and sat beside him on the charpai. 'Then show them again. With me watching the whole time.' Imran rolled his eyes, but he opened it.

passage: I'm Afreen, a teaching assistant for the first-year coding course, and I've been watching Sangeeta all semester. passage: Harsha, you want to put the Hindi-medium and English-medium sections together for annual day and 'let them mix'. Let me tell you what happened when I tried that in 1989, at a girls' school in Mangalore. I put both sections in one hall to rehearse: English-medium girls on stage with the lines, Kannada-medium girls in the chorus at the back. No shared goal, just one group decorating the other's show. By the third day they had names for each other. One girl cried in the washroom. I thought mixing would do the magic. It made things worse. The next year, Elizabeth Teacher got wiser. I gave them one play to write together, in both languages, with equal parts and one rule: no mocking, or you're out. The principal sat in on rehearsals. That play is still the best thing I ever directed.

qa.q: Where did Elizabeth try this in 1989?
qa.a: At a girls' school in Mangalore.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when a girl cried in the washroom?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt dismayed and guilty, realising the hoped-for mixing had made things worse.

qa.q: The next year Elizabeth gave both sections one play to write together, with equal parts. Why was that a turning point?
qa.a: It gave the girls a shared goal and equal status, with clear backing from the principal, so contact built respect instead of names.

qa.q: What was it like for the Kannada-medium girls in the back chorus?
qa.a: They probably felt looked down on and unequal, decorating someone else's show, which bred resentment.

grounding: A senior teacher recalls contact between two groups failing without shared goals or equal roles, and what worked instead.

passage:
Saturday night.
We WON the inter-school science fair!!! A water filter from coconut husk and sand. When Ma'am put me with Nandini and the two boys from the municipal school across the tracks, I sulked. Everyone in my building says those kids are rough and don't study. I even told Ma'am it wasn't fair. But I can't build a filter frame, and Nandini can; her father's a carpenter. She can't do the presentation in English, and I can. Imran worked out the sand layers, and Sachin got the coconut husks from his uncle's shop. For three weeks we ate lunch together every day because we HAD to. Today, when the judges called us, Nandini hugged me and I didn't even think about it. I think I was the rough one, in my head.
Lokesh

qa.q: What did the team build?
qa.a: A water filter from coconut husk and sand.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when first put in the team?
qa.a: Lokesh felt resentful and sulky, having absorbed the building's idea that the municipal school kids were rough.

qa.q: What made this team change Lokesh's views more than a talk would have?
qa.a: Each member needed the others' skills to win, so weeks of shared effort replaced stereotypes with real knowledge.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt when the judges called them?
qa.a: Nandini was probably overjoyed and proud, hugging Lokesh as a real teammate.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows a science-fair team from different neighbourhoods turning 'them' into 'us' through shared effort.

passage: In the town of Chengannur, the boys from the church side and the boys from the temple side had never shared a bench. So when the district science contest needed a four-member team to build a solar water pump, and the teacher picked Thomas and Eshaan with two others, both groaned. Eshaan knew circuits; Thomas's father repaired boat engines, and Thomas knew motors. Neither could do the whole thing. For a month they stayed after school in the lab, arguing, borrowing each other's tools, sharing lunch when the power went off. The night before the contest the pump leaked. Thomas held the pipe; Eshaan soldered by phone torch. It worked at 11 pm. They walked home together as far as the fork in the road, then stood there another half hour, talking.

qa.q: What did the team have to build?
qa.a: A solar water pump.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel when first picked with Thomas?
qa.a: Eshaan felt reluctant and resentful, groaning at being teamed with a boy from the other side.

qa.q: Why did this project change how the boys saw each other?
qa.a: Each needed the other's skill, circuits and motors, to reach a common goal, so working as equals built respect.

qa.q: What might Thomas feel standing at the fork in the road?
qa.a: Thomas probably feels a new closeness and pride, unwilling to end the talk with someone he had never shared a bench with.

grounding: In a small town two teenagers from different communities depend on each other to build a pump and become friends.

passage:
Lab mentor's note, first-year biology batch, October.
Sabina is the only student from Kashmir in this batch. In the first weeks she was asked the same questions over and over, at the bench and in the canteen: about 'the situation', about what 'people there' think. She answered patiently, then began arriving just before class and leaving immediately. She told me, 'I'm tired of being a news report.' Her lab partner, Tushar, changed things more than I did. He asked which cricket team she supports, argued with her about the spice in the canteen rajma and teased her pipetting. Last week she stayed for tea after the practical. I have asked the batch to keep their questions for the person, not the region, and I'll check in with Sabina next month.

qa.q: What did Sabina say she was tired of being?
qa.a: A news report.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel after weeks of the same questions?
qa.a: Sabina felt tired and somewhat resentful, burdened with representing a whole region, so she began avoiding the batch.

qa.q: Why was asking the batch to keep questions for the person a good step?
qa.a: It helps classmates treat Sabina as an individual rather than a spokesperson, easing the pressure on her.

qa.q: How does Tushar help change things?
qa.a: Tushar treats Sabina as a person, arguing about rajma and teasing her pipetting, which makes her feel like an ordinary classmate.

grounding: A mentor notes a student who is the only one from her region, tired of representing it, until ordinary contact lets her be herself.

Wednesday night.
Week three at the Delhi internship. I'm the only one from Tamil Nadu on the floor, and everyone's very curious. Today someone called me 'our Madrasi' again (I'm from Madurai), someone asked if I eat only idli, and in the meeting the manager said, 'Pooja, tell us how south Indians see this.' As if I'm the ambassador for five states! I smiled through it, but I'm so tired of explaining everyone. On the phone, Amma, Nirmala the wise, said, 'Kanna, find the one person who asks about you.' And there is one: Jaspreet, who asked what music I like and now sends me songs. With her I'm just Pooja who hates spreadsheets. Tomorrow I'll eat lunch with her again.
Pooja

qa.a: From Madurai.

passage:
Department head's note, customer support floor, quarterly review.
Tenzin took over as team lead in March, inheriting a floor split into a Hindi-speaking team, a Kannada-speaking team and the north-east hires, who sat in a corner. Jokes about accents were common. Tenzin did not give a lecture. He rebuilt the teams: each pod now has members from all three groups, a shared weekly target and rotating pod leaders. He posted one rule on the board, 'No mocking anyone's language or home', and enforced it the first time it was broken, with a quiet word and a written warning. Maria, from the old corner, now leads a pod and trains others on escalations. Complaints are down and the pods compete happily. Next: I have asked Tenzin to present this approach at the managers' meeting.

qa.q: What rule did Tenzin post on the board?
qa.a: 'No mocking anyone's language or home.'

qa.q: What does Tenzin's quick enforcement of the rule suggest about his attitude?
qa.a: It suggests Tenzin felt firm and determined that mockery would not be tolerated, taking fairness seriously.

qa.q: Why did rebuilding the teams work better than a lecture?
qa.a: Mixed pods with a shared target and equal, rotating roles let people work together as equals, which softens attitudes.

qa.q: How might Maria's experience of the floor have changed?
qa.a: Maria has gone from sitting in the corner to leading a pod and training others, so she likely feels respected and part of the team.

grounding: A department head notes a young team lead who builds mixed teams with shared goals and equal roles and stops mockery.

passage:
Tuesday.
Big day. I finally changed the project groups. For months my team of twelve at the design firm had split in two, the metro-college hires and the small-town hires, and the jokes had started. 'Bhupen, explain it in simple words for your people.' I hated it and said nothing, which was cowardly. Today I made four mixed groups of three, each with the same client brief and equal roles, lead, researcher and presenter, rotating every week. And I said one thing clearly in the meeting: 'Joke about the work, never about where someone's from. That's final.' Bhupen looked up, surprised. By evening his group was arguing happily about fonts. I don't expect everyone to change overnight. But I've seen it before: people who build something together stop sneering.
Nikita, stay firm.

qa.q: How many mixed groups did Nikita make?
qa.a: Four mixed groups of three.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel about staying silent for months?
qa.a: Nikita felt ashamed, calling the silence cowardly.

qa.q: What makes Nikita's new plan likely to soften attitudes?
qa.a: Mixed groups with the same brief, rotating equal roles and a firm rule against mocking create equal-status teamwork backed by the lead.

qa.q: How might Bhupen feel after the meeting?
qa.a: Bhupen was surprised and likely relieved to have the lead stand against the jokes, and seems happier arguing about fonts.

grounding: A young team lead's diary shows her forming mixed groups with a shared goal and equal roles, and banning mockery.
